headings.title: Introduction to Postnatal Care and Follow-up
headings.content: Postnatal care (PNC) and follow-up represent a crucial phase in maternal and child health, starting immediately after the birth of the baby and extending through the first six weeks, often referred to as the puerperium. In the context of nursing practice in Nigeria, this period is vital for reducing maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality rates, which remain significant public health concerns. The transition to motherhood involves immense physical, emotional, and social adjustments. Follow-up care ensures that both the mother and the newborn are recovering safely from the labor and delivery process. Nurses play a frontline role in delivering this care, acting as educators, advocates, and clinical assessors. Postnatal follow-up provides an opportunity to detect early warning signs of complications such as postpartum hemorrhage, infection, and hypertensive disorders. Furthermore, it bridges the gap between hospital-based delivery and community reintegration, establishing continuity of care. By empowering mothers with knowledge regarding danger signs, proper nutrition, and infant care, nursing professionals lay the foundation for a healthy family and community. Comprehensive postnatal care addresses not just physical healing, but also psychological well-being, infant feeding support, and the integration of culturally sensitive health practices prevalent in Nigeria.

headings.title: Physiological Changes and Puerperal Recovery
headings.content: Puerperal recovery involves profound physiological adjustments as the maternal body returns to its pre-pregnant state. One of the primary processes is involution, which is the rapid reduction in the size of the uterus following placental delivery. Nurses must monitor fundal height, which should decrease by approximately one centimeter daily, descending into the pelvic cavity by about two weeks postpartum. Uterine contractions, often experienced as afterpains, help achieve hemostasis at the placental site and are particularly noticeable during breastfeeding due to oxytocin release. Vaginal discharge, known as lochia, transitions through distinct stages: lochia rubra (red, lasting 1-3 days), lochia serosa (pinkish-brown, lasting 4-10 days), and lochia alba (whitish-yellow, lasting up to 3-6 weeks). Any foul odor, heavy bleeding, or reversion to bright red lochia can signify complications such as retained placental tissue or endometrium infection. Additionally, the cardiovascular system undergoes shifts in blood volume and cardiac output, while the urinary system may experience diuresis and potential trauma or bladder atony. Lactogenesis begins as hormonal levels shift post-placental expulsion, leading to breast engorgement and milk production. Understanding these normal physiological changes enables nurses to differentiate between normal recovery processes and pathological deviations.

headings.title: Schedule of Routine Postnatal Visits
headings.content: A structured schedule of routine postnatal visits is essential for proactive healthcare management during the puerperium. The World Health Organization (WHO) and national guidelines recommend specific contact points to ensure maternal and neonatal safety. The first critical contact occurs within 24 hours of birth, followed by subsequent visits at 48 to 72 hours, between 7 to 14 days, and a final comprehensive postnatal check at 6 weeks postpartum. For mothers who delivered at home or left a facility early, a visit within the first 24 hours is paramount to identify immediate life-threatening complications like postpartum hemorrhage or severe neonatal hypothermia. The 48-to-72-hour visit coincides with the physiological drop in neonatal bilirubin and the onset of copious milk production (ogba/engorgement phase). The 2-week visit allows nurses to evaluate wound healing from cesarean sections or perineal repairs, check breastfeeding efficacy, and screen for early mood disturbances. The 6-week final visit serves as a comprehensive milestone to evaluate complete physical involution, discuss family planning options, administer routine immunizations, and clear the mother for resumption of sexual activity and normal daily routines. Adhering to this structured timeline ensures optimal health outcomes and early interventions.

headings.title: Comprehensive Maternal Assessment
headings.content: Comprehensive maternal assessment during postnatal follow-up requires a systematic head-to-toe physical evaluation combined with psychosocial screening. The nurse begins by taking a thorough history regarding maternal perception of her recovery, sleep patterns, emotional state, and any pain levels. Vital signs must be strictly monitored: persistent pyrexia can indicate endometritis or urinary tract infection, hypertension may point to postpartum preeclampsia, and tachycardia can be an early sign of hemorrhage or sepsis. Abdominal palpation is performed to check fundal height, tone, and tenderness. The perineum or abdominal surgical incision must be inspected using the REEDA scale (Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge, Approximation) to ensure proper healing and rule out hematoma or wound dehiscence. Breast assessment is vital to check for symmetry, cracked nipples, blocked ducts, or signs of mastitis. Elimination patterns are evaluated, checking for postpartum diuresis, urinary retention, and bowel function, particularly the passage of flatus and the prevention of constipation. Lower extremities are inspected for signs of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), including unilateral swelling, pain, and positive Homan's sign, although clinical judgment is advised. Finally, assessing lochia amount, color, and odor completes the physical examination.

headings.title: Newborn Evaluation and Neonatal Care
headings.content: Newborn evaluation and neonatal care during postnatal follow-up aim to promote growth, development, and prevent neonatal morbidity. Nurses conduct a thorough physical examination of the neonate, checking vital signs, skin color (monitoring for jaundice), hydration status, and umbilical cord healing. Weight is measured to ensure the baby is recovering from the normal physiological weight loss (which should not exceed 10% of birth weight) and is gaining weight steadily by day 10 to 14. Feeding assessment is a cornerstone of neonatal care; the nurse observes breastfeeding technique, latch, suck-swallow coordination, and infant satisfaction. For mothers choosing formula feeding, nurses educate on safe preparation, sterilization, and volume requirements. Cord care education emphasizes keeping the cord stump clean and dry, avoiding traditional concoctions or harmful substances that can introduce tetanus or bacterial infections. Thermoregulation is closely monitored, teaching parents how to dress the baby appropriately and practice Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) where applicable, especially for low birth weight infants. Additionally, nurses verify administration of birth doses of vaccines such as BCG, oral polio vaccine (OPV 0), and Hepatitis B, while scheduling subsequent immunization dates.

headings.title: Identification and Management of Postnatal Complications
headings.content: The identification and management of postnatal complications require sharp clinical vigilance from nursing professionals. Postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) remains a leading cause of maternal mortality; nurses must remain alert to delayed PPH caused by subinvolution or retained products of conception. Puerperal sepsis is another critical hazard, often presenting with fever, chills, lower abdominal pain, and foul-smelling lochia; early detection, administration of prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics, and supportive care are essential. Hypertensive disorders, such as postpartum preeclampsia, can develop or persist after delivery, manifesting as high blood pressure, severe headaches, visual disturbances, and epigastric pain, requiring prompt medical referral and monitoring. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) resulting from bladder catheterization or residual urine stasis are managed with hydration and antibiotics. Breast complications like engorgement, plugged ducts, and mastitis require immediate intervention involving proper milk expression, warm compresses, and antibiotic therapy if infectious mastitis is established. Nurses must educate women and their families on red-flag symptoms so they know when to seek emergency medical attention without delay, reducing the risk of permanent morbidity or mortality.

headings.title: Mental Health Screening and Postpartum Depression
headings.content: Mental health screening is an integral component of holistic postnatal follow-up, as the postpartum period carries a significant vulnerability for mood disorders. Nurses must distinguish between 'baby blues,' which is mild, transient mood instability affecting up to 80% of new mothers due to hormonal shifts and fatigue, and clinical postpartum depression (PPD). Baby blues typically resolve within two weeks without formal psychiatric intervention, requiring reassurance, rest, and family support. Conversely, postpartum depression presents with persistent sadness, severe anxiety, feelings of worthlessness, inability to care for oneself or the infant, and intrusive thoughts, lasting beyond two weeks. Utilizing validated screening tools like the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) during routine visits enables nurses to identify at-risk mothers early. In severe cases, postpartum psychosis may occur—a psychiatric emergency characterized by hallucinations, delusions, and bizarre behavior, which demands immediate psychiatric hospitalization. Nursing interventions involve compassionate listening, non-judgmental counseling, dismantling social stigmas surrounding mental health in Nigerian communities, and connecting families with specialized mental health resources and support networks.

headings.title: Family Planning and Contraceptive Counseling
headings.content: Family planning and contraceptive counseling are essential topics that must be integrated into postnatal follow-up care to promote maternal health, child spacing, and overall family well-being. Nurses provide tailored education regarding the return of fertility, explaining that ovulation can resume even before the return of regular menstruation or while exclusively breastfeeding. The Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) is an effective natural family planning option for mothers who are fully or nearly fully breastfeeding, whose infants are under six months of age, and whose menses have not returned. For those requiring alternative methods, nurses discuss hormonal options such as progestogen-only pills (POPs), injectables (e.g., Depo-Provera), implants (e.g., Jadelle, Implanon), and barrier methods like condoms. For postpartum women, progestogen-only contraceptives are generally preferred during lactation as they do not interfere with breast milk supply or quality, unlike combined oral contraceptives which are deferred due to thromboembolic risks in early puerperium. Intrauterine devices (IUDs) can also be inserted postplacental or at the 6-week visit following careful clinical assessment. Counseling must be confidential, voluntary, culturally sensitive, and respectful of the couple's reproductive goals.

headings.title: Nutrition, Self-Care, and Health Education
headings.content: Nutrition, self-care, and targeted health education empower postnatal mothers to regain their strength and care effectively for their newborns. Nutritional counseling emphasizes the increased caloric and fluid demands of lactation, encouraging a balanced diet rich in protein, iron, calcium, and essential vitamins to replenish nutrient stores depleted during pregnancy and childbirth. In the Nigerian context, incorporating locally available, nutrient-dense foods is crucial for practical adherence. Self-care education covers adequate rest, pelvic floor exercises (Kegel exercises) to restore muscular tone and prevent urinary incontinence, and proper hygiene regarding perineal care and breast care. Nurses also counsel families on danger signs that necessitate immediate return to the health facility, such as heavy vaginal bleeding, severe lower abdominal pain, high fever, foul lochia, breathing difficulties, and calf pain. Environmental safety, prevention of postpartum fatigue, and the involvement of partners and extended family members in supportive roles are discussed to foster a nurturing home environment. Through empathetic and structured health education, nurses ensure that mothers transition smoothly into their new roles with confidence and resilience.
